https://www.baltictimes.com/entrepreneur.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Entrepreneurs for Peace opens civil-military cooperation Hub in Riga 2026-07-22 On 21 July, the Entrepreneurs for Peace Foundation opened a new Civil-Military Cooperation Hub in Riga. The hub will serve as a meeting place for entrepreneurs, public institutions, non-governmental organisations and members of the public to work together to strengthen Latvia's resilience and continue supporting Ukraine. The hub will foster cooperation with developers of military products and services, support new initiatives aimed at strengthening Latvia's security, and bring together the foundation's partners to develop joint solutions. It will also host events and educational activities designed to increase public awareness of national defence, societal resilience and preparedness to respond to crises. During the opening event, the foundation highlighted three key messages: the importance of cooperation, the need to remain vigilant, and the achievements made to date, demonstrating that civic initiatives can make a significant contribution to strengthening Latvia's security while continuing to support Ukraine. "Over the past four and a half years, we have shown that the greatest results can be achieved by working together with Latvian businesses, strategic partners, non-governmental organisations and active members of society. The foundation will continue supporting Ukraine while placing increasing emphasis on strengthening Latvia's resilience and implementing new initiatives that will enhance the country's ability to respond to hybrid threats," said Laura Skrodele, Director of the Entrepreneurs for Peace Foundation. She added that the new hub is intended to become a place where cooperation is transformed into practical action and thanked the foundation's partners, without whose support its work would not have been possible. Speaking about the security situation, representatives of the foundation stressed that Russia's war against Ukraine continues and that security challenges in Europe have not diminished. Ukrainian civilians continue to suffer daily attacks, while Latvia must further strengthen its resilience and preparedness for a wide range of security threats. Since 2022, Entrepreneurs for Peace has delivered more than €23 million worth of assistance to Ukraine, including 1,000 drones, 300 generators, 1,300 vehicles, and 1,200 units of medical and technical equipment. The organization has also supported Latvian volunteers serving in Ukraine, implemented social infrastructure reconstruction projects in Ukraine's Chernihiv region, and organized humanitarian aid convoys in cooperation with the Latvian State Police, the National Armed Forces and numerous Latvian companies. The importance of civil-military cooperation was also highlighted by Colonel Volodymyr Rusinov , Commander of the 26th Artillery Brigade, who emphasized that close cooperation between the armed forces, businesses and society is essential for strengthening national security. "Modern security depends not only on the capabilities of the armed forces but also on the willingness of society as a whole to participate and cooperate. Civil-military cooperation is one of the cornerstones of national resilience, and initiatives such as this strengthen our collective ability to respond to security challenges. I would like to thank the Entrepreneurs for Peace Foundation for its selfless and consistently timely support to Ukraine and its soldiers," said Colonel Rusinov. Latvian volunteer fighter Aleksandrs Sverčkovs , who had recently returned from Ukraine, shared his experiences from the front line and emphasized the importance of public support for those defending Ukraine every day. "On the front line, what you feel most is that every soldier is backed by people who genuinely care. Every donation, every shipment of aid and every word of encouragement give us the strength to keep fighting," said A. Sverčkovs. Ieva Vārna, who had also recently returned from the Donbas region, spoke about the situation in Ukraine and stressed that international support remains critically important. "After what I witnessed in Donbas, one thing is clear: the war is far from over, and Ukraine still needs our support every single day. Everyone who gets involved truly helps save lives," said I. Vārna. The event concluded with remarks by the foundation's chaplain, Elmārs Pļaviņš , Senior Expert on International Military Religious Affairs at the Ministry of Defence, who thanked the organisation's partners for their trust and long-standing cooperation. "Every step we take together proves that we are not alone. Thank you to every partner whose work and support help strengthen both Latvia and Ukraine," said E. Pļaviņš. Viesturs Silenieks also introduced guests to the activities of Drone House and the opportunities offered by the new hub, inviting participants on a guided tour of the centre's main areas of operation. About Entrepreneurs for Peace Since 2022, the Entrepreneurs for Peace Foundation has brought together entrepreneurs and partners to provide practical support to Ukraine while strengthening Latvia's security and societal resilience. The organisation coordinates humanitarian and military assistance deliveries, works closely with public authorities, and implements projects that advance civil-military cooperation. https://allafrica.com/stories/2026082000.text: Namibia: Vet Budget Puts Beef Exports At Risk The Directorate of Veterinary Services (DVS) in the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform has exhausted its 2026/27 operational budget, putting prerequisite European Union (EU) export farm inspections under pressure. According to the Namibia Agricultural Union (NAU), EU-approved livestock farms must undergo annual inspections by a state veterinarian to maintain their EU certification and, with it, access to important export markets. "However, these inspections came to a halt earlier this year after the DVS said its operational budget for this service had been exhausted," the NAU says. This placed producers who export to the EU under considerable pressure. If inspections are not carried out on time, certification may lapse, and producers may no longer be able to slaughter livestock at export-approved abattoirs. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines "This could in turn, affect the industry, the abattoirs, and Namibia's ability to meet its international export obligations," the NAU says. EU chargé d'affaires Ian Dupont says trade in livestock and animal products is necessarily subject to strict sanitary and phytosanitary, animal-health and food safety requirements. "These requirements are intended to protect the importing country from risks such as the introduction or spread of animal diseases, food-borne hazards, residues and other risks associated with products of animal origin," he says. The DVS must have an effective system of registration, traceability, disease surveillance inspection and certification covering the animals, he adds. "For the farmer, the simplest way of looking at it is that the health guarantee attached to a piece of Namibian beef exported to Europe starts on the farm, not at the abattoir," Dupont says. Approximately 1 500 to 2 000 Namibian producers supplying or wishing to supply animals into the EU export chain undergo these inspections each year, Dupont says. The Livestock Producers Organisation (LPO) urgently brought the matter to the relevant role-players and following discussions between organised agriculture, DVS and the Livestock and Livestock Products Board, a temporary solution has been reached to prevent disruption to exports. Dupont says the inspection interval is determined by the level of risk and that, in Namibia's case, where transboundary livestock diseases such as foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) and bovine lung sickness occur in the region, inspections are required at least annually. Russian President Vladimir Putin originally extended the invitation last month. On Wednesday, Foreign Policy Advisor Yury Ushakov said the invitation stands but that no Europeans have so far agreed to embark on the diplomatic sojourn. Russia's Ambassador to Germany Sergei Nechayev on Wednesday told France's AFP news agency that reaction to Putin's invitation has been "restrained." Nechayev claimed that Moscow remains, "ready to continue the dialogue and carry on with negotiations." He also repeated the Kremlin claim that it is Europe that is the impediment to stopping the war, and that Russia — which launched and continues to execute its unprovoked years-long war of aggression in Ukraine — is the only party truly interested in peace. Nechayev said the Kremlin doesn't see the same "honesty" from the Europeans that it does from US President Donald Trump's team — made up of his son-in-law Jared Kushner and his friend Steve Witkoff — and wants to "know precisely what their intentions are." Russia has been accused of foot dragging as a way to prolong attacks on Ukraine. On Wednesday, Nechayev continued in that vein, saying: "Our request to Europe is this: Decide what it is you want, determine whom you will appoint as negotiators, and, most importantly, clarify what you aim to achieve." "An ordinance is already being prepared by the government and should enter into force at the end of December or the beginning of January," said Tomczyk. "We will also urge our allies — the ⁠entire ​NATO alliance — to establish such a ​principle along the eastern flank," he continued, "Poland was a pioneer ​in this regard, ‌and the Baltic states have since followed our lead." Poland strictly limits air traffic at its border already. On Wednesday, Tomczyk said the proposed no-fly zone will cover several dozen kilometers of territory from the border and provide added support for Poland's armed forces. Merz tackled criticism from opposition parties on the left and right head on, saying "Russia knows exactly ​what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine." "Russia is escalating in the Baltic region, in Poland, on the Black Sea. Russia ​is escalating ‌in space. And Russia is now escalating massively here, in our own country, too, even at the risk of loss of life," he added. Merz said, "anyone who doesn't see that, doesn't understand the world around them, or they are pursuing entirely different aims." The Left Party and Alternative for Germany (AfD) have both called for an end to Ukraine aid and better relations with Moscow . Among other things, Germany blames Russia for an explosive drone incident at Leipzig airport this summer as well as cyberattacks, sabotage and airspace incursions across the EU and NATO . Merz said on Wednesday that by supporting Ukraine, Germany is protecting itself. "We are learning from Ukraine," said Merz, "technologically for civilian use but of course also in defense ⁠technology." The Day with Terry Martin: Why is support for Ukraine down in Germany? Russia again focused its attacks on Ukraine's energy structure in an attempt to break the will of the country's civilian population as the bitter cold of winter sets in . Moscow's troops attacked a thermal energy power plant, shutting it down; as well as targeting a gas production facility in Poltawa, where ensuing fires also shut down operations. Ukraine's acting energy minister said that power outages were reported in five regions as a result of the Russian attacks. In Russia's Samara region, Ukrainian drones hit at least two oil refineries, killing one person, sparking large fires and and causing energy blackouts. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Kyiv was justified in its actions because it has an "absolute right to self-defense." Libya on Wednesday announced that two of its soldiers had died from injuries sustained during a weekend drone attack that sank a Russian warship. Speaking with French broadcaster TF1, Barrot said, "For nearly five years now, [Russian President] Vladimir Putin has not only been bombing Ukraine, but has also been constantly engaging in acts of aggression and harassing Europeans in an attempt to undermine our unity." Barrot said Russia alone is to blame for the war and its expansion, and then asked, "What would we do if we were being bombarded day and night by an enemy — an invader?" Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani on Wednesday criticized Kyiv's actions, saying, "It was a mistake to violate Libya's sovereignty" and warned against further similar activities in other regions. Speaking with Italy's Corriere della Sera newspaper ‌on ⁠Wednesday, Tajani said, "Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv's intentions to strike in ​Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port." Tajani said he had spoken with Ukraine Foreign Minister Andrii Sybihato and conveyed Italy's concern over the matter, adding that Rome would continue its staunch support for Ukraine and its sovereignty while at the same time seeking to keep the conflict from spreading.
